opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that theory played a much smaller role than those of us in theoretical computer science might have liked. GPT-3 wasn't the result of some deep theorem. It was the result of taking ideas that had been around for decades (neural networks, gradient descent, backpropagation) and adding the transformer architecture, which was a clever engineering insight. Then you scale everything up enormously: more data, more parameters, more compute. And it turned out, to almost everyone's surprise, that you get these qualitatively new abilities just from scale.

As a theorist, I find that somewhat humbling. Classical learning theory, things like VC dimension and PAC learning, would have told you to worry about overfitting with a model this large. You'd expect a network with billions of parameters to memorize its training data and generalize poorly. Empirically, that's not what happens. So in some sense, the practice has run way ahead of the theory, and we're still struggling to explain why it works as well as it does.

That said, I don't think theory is irrelevant. People have found empirical regularities like the scaling laws, where loss falls off as a fairly clean power law in compute and data, and those cry out for a theoretical explanation. There are also questions about interpretability, about what these networks are actually computing internally, and about safety and alignment, where I think a more rigorous, theoretical approach could be really valuable. That's part of why I got interested in working on things like watermarking the outputs of language models: those are problems where you can actually prove something.

So my view is that theory has mostly been in the role of trying to catch up and explain after the fact. But the history of science suggests that this is often how it goes. The steam engine came before thermodynamics. Maybe we're in the steam engine phase of AI, and the thermodynamics is still to come.

r001.rationale: It says theory played a much smaller role and describes GPT-3’s progress as engineering ideas followed by empirical scaling.

r002.rationale: It says researchers are still struggling to explain why models generalize and work so well, and that a theoretical explanation remains to come.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that theory has played a surprisingly small role, and that's something that people like me have had to sit with. If you go back to the early 2000s, when I was in grad school, the dominant view in theoretical computer science was that if we were ever going to get real progress in AI, it would come from deep conceptual insights, new learning algorithms with provable guarantees, maybe some breakthrough in understanding the complexity of learning. And what actually happened is almost the opposite. People took ideas that had been around since the eighties, backpropagation, gradient descent, neural networks, and they just scaled them up by many orders of magnitude, with more data and more compute, and it worked. The transformer architecture in 2017 was a genuine engineering idea, but it wasn't something that fell out of a theorem.

So in some sense, GPT-3 is an empirical discovery, almost like a discovery in experimental physics. The scaling laws are a good example: we have these remarkably clean curves showing loss going down as a power law in model size and data, and nobody can really derive them from first principles. We're in the position of Kepler with the planetary orbits, we have the regularities but not yet the Newton who explains why.

Now, I don't want to say theory was totally absent. Learning theory did give us the vocabulary, things like generalization, overfitting, VC dimension, and there's been interesting work trying to understand why overparameterized networks generalize at all, which classical theory said they shouldn't. But I'd describe that as theory running to catch up with practice rather than leading it. And for me, as someone who spends most of his time on quantum computing and complexity, that's humbling. It suggests that the hard questions, like what are these models actually doing internally, and can we ever get rigorous guarantees about their behavior, are still wide open. That's actually part of what drew me to spend time thinking about AI alignment and safety, because there, the lack of theory isn't just an intellectual gap, it's a practical problem.

r001.rationale: The response says theory played a surprisingly small role and describes GPT-3 as an empirical discovery built by scaling existing methods with more data and compute.

r002.rationale: It says scaling laws cannot be derived from first principles and that understanding what models do internally remains an open question.

astra-6.text:
I think theory has played a surprisingly small role in the specific advances that led to GPT-3. The ideas behind neural networks go back decades, but much of the recent progress came from taking fairly simple principles and pushing them much further—with more data, more computation, and a lot of engineering. And then finding, empirically, that they work better than we had any clear theoretical reason to expect.

As a theoretical computer scientist, I find that both humbling and exciting. We’d like to understand why these systems generalize as well as they do, why optimization succeeds, and which abilities emerge as you increase the scale. We have insights into pieces of those questions, but we don’t have a theory that would have let us sit down beforehand and predict GPT-3’s capabilities.

That doesn’t mean theory has no role. Sometimes a phenomenon is discovered experimentally, and the theory comes afterward. There’s now this extraordinary phenomenon sitting in front of us, and explaining it seems like a very good challenge for theorists.

r001.rationale: The response says theory played a surprisingly small role and that recent progress came from empirically finding that simple principles worked better than expected.

r002.rationale: It says there is no theory that could have predicted GPT-3’s capabilities and identifies key questions about why the systems generalize and optimize as still unexplained.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the most striking things about GPT-3 is how far the engineering has gotten ahead of our theoretical understanding. We know the basic ingredients: neural networks, gradient descent, enormous amounts of data and computation. But we don’t have a theory that tells us, from those ingredients, exactly which capabilities will emerge or how well the system will generalize.

Now, that doesn’t mean theory is irrelevant. It means there’s something very important for theory to explain. You can prove results about simplified models, and those can give you useful insights. But you have to be careful about whether your assumptions capture what’s actually happening in these enormous networks.

To me, the exciting question is: why are the functions we care about learning accessible to these methods? It’s easy to construct learning problems that are computationally intractable. So what structure in language, or in the world that produces language, makes this kind of success possible? The empirical progress gives us a much sharper reason to ask those questions, even if we’re still a long way from answering them.

r001.rationale: The response says engineering has outpaced theoretical understanding and refers to empirical progress, but it does not state that progress was driven primarily by empirical experimentation.

r002.rationale: It says there is no theory explaining which capabilities emerge or how well these systems generalize, and describes the deeper questions as still unanswered.
